name: Market Beta
description:
How much of the move belongs to the
market?
Beta measures the slope of an asset's historical return response to a specified benchmark.
Samjho: the question is how strongly the asset usually reacts, not whether its latest candle
looks impressive.
method:
β_i,m = Cov(r_i, r_m) / Var(r_m).
OLS: r_i,t = α + β r_m,t + e_t.
OLS with intercept on synchronized simple UTC-daily returns; sample covariance uses n-1.
interpretation:
The screen shows SOL outperforming BTC. The model shows that most of the difference is
consistent with higher beta. The remaining 0.4 points are a model residual, not proof of
informed buying.

name: The hidden identity: Beta = Correlation x Volatility Ratio
description:
Separate shared direction from
amplified volatility
The beta identity splits sensitivity into correlation and relative volatility. Two assets can have
the same beta for very different reasons: one tracks BTC closely; another is volatile but only
loosely connected.
method:
β = ρ_i,m * (σ_i / σ_m).
Algebraic identity using covariance-consistent sample correlation and standard deviations.
interpretation:
AVAX may look like a stronger BTC proxy. Its lower correlation means much of its volatility is
unrelated to BTC; sizing from beta alone misses that residual risk.

name: BTC Beta
description:
Read the altcoin through the BTC anchor
BTC beta isolates sensitivity to Bitcoin returns. It is useful for market exposure and hedging
research, but it cannot absorb every technology, sector or token-supply event.
method:
β_i,BTC = Cov(r_i, r_BTC) / Var(r_BTC).
BTC is the benchmark; UTC-daily simple returns in the stated case.
interpretation:
The apparent BTC-led decline contains additional LINK weakness. Confirmed venue selling
supports a supply explanation, while the depositor's intent remains unknown.

name: ETH Beta
description:
Choose the benchmark that matches the
business
ETH beta asks how an asset responds to Ethereum. For ecosystem research it may add context
beyond BTC, although separate single-factor betas do not identify independent causal effects.
method:
β_i,ETH = Cov(r_i, r_ETH) / Var(r_ETH).
ETH is the benchmark; use when smart-contract ecosystem exposure is the research question.
interpretation:
ARB appears to lead the market. Much of the move may belong to a shared Ethereum theme;
the approximate 0.46-point remainder still needs transaction and liquidity evidence.

name: Total Crypto Market Beta
description:
Measure exposure to a defined crypto
universe
Total-market beta depends on the index as much as the asset. Weights, stablecoins, wrapped
duplicates and stale prices decide what the phrase market return actually means.
method:
β_i,MKT = Cov(r_i, r_MKT) / Var(r_MKT).
Total-crypto benchmark return must be a documented investable or research index; never regress price levels.
interpretation:
Broad-market outperformance is meaningful only against a documented universe. A
stablecoin-heavy index can mechanically make volatile tokens look unusually strong.

name: Sector Beta
description:
Distinguish sector participation from
token leadership
Sector beta compares an asset with economically related peers. A leave-one-out basket
prevents the token from explaining itself, while liquidity screens stop stale peers from
distorting the comparison.
method:
β_i,sector = Cov(r_i, r_sector) / Var(r_sector).
Sector basket weights and rebalancing rules are frozen in metadata before estimation.
interpretation:
AAVE is participating strongly in a sector move. The evidence does not yet justify calling every
percentage point protocol-specific repricing.

name: Multi Factor Beta
description:
Decompose the candle into competing
factors
Multiple regression estimates conditional exposures simultaneously. Each coefficient describes
the incremental association with one factor after accounting for the others in the chosen
model.
method:
r_i,t = α + β_1 f_1,t + ... + β_K f_K,t + e_t. OLS: b_hat=(X'X)^(-1)X'y.
OLS with intercept; factors expressed in stationary changes/returns and aligned without look-ahead.
interpretation:
The screen suggests isolated momentum. The decomposition suggests common BTC and
ETH-related forces plus an unresolved residual.

name: Rolling Beta
description:
Watch the sensitivity change beneath the
price
Rolling beta repeats the same estimator on trailing windows. It exposes changing exposure, but
adjacent estimates share observations and are not independent discoveries.
method:
β_t(W) = Cov_W(r_i,r_m) / Var_W(r_m), using observations t-W+1,...,t.
Trailing rolling window; example W=90 observations, no centered windows in live automation.
interpretation:
The market may be showing an unusually weak coin; part of the decline could be ordinary
exposure under a newly higher beta regime.

name: Upside Beta
description:
Measure participation when BTC rises
Upside beta estimates the return slope only on positive benchmark periods. It describes
conditional sensitivity, which is different from averaging positive asset returns.
method:
β_up = Cov(r_i,r_m | r_m>0) / Var(r_m | r_m>0).
Conditional OLS/covariance on benchmark-positive observations only.
interpretation:
INJ's rally is broadly consistent with its historical upside response. Whether it keeps that gain
during stress is a separate research question.

name: Downside Beta
description:
Find the exposure that appears in a
selloff
Downside beta estimates sensitivity on negative BTC periods. It makes asymmetric exposure
visible, but it is not a worst-loss bound or a liquidation model.
method:
β_down = Cov(r_i,r_m | r_m<0) / Var(r_m | r_m<0).
Conditional OLS/covariance on benchmark-negative observations only.
interpretation:
The red candle is not fully explained by BTC. Thin depth may amplify the remaining weakness
without requiring a coordinated attack.

name: Bull Regime Beta
description:
Test exposure inside a declared uptrend
Bull-regime beta restricts estimation to a predeclared market state. Here the state is known at
the previous close: BTC above its trailing 60-close average.
method:
β_bull = Cov(r_i, r_BTC | B_t=1) / Var(r_BTC | B_t=1).
B_t = 1 if BTC close_(t-1) > SMA60_(t-1).
House regime rule, fixed before the measured return; strict inequality. A tie is unclassified. OLS with intercept within the state.
interpretation:
The regime helps organize evidence, not certify a bull market. RENDER's additional strength
remains an attribution problem.

name: Bear Regime Beta
description:
Re-estimate sensitivity when the market
is defensive
Bear-regime beta uses periods classified as weak before their returns occur. It tests whether a
holding becomes more sensitive precisely when portfolio diversification matters.
method:
β_bear = Cov(r_i, r_BTC | D_t=1) / Var(r_BTC | D_t=1).
D_t = 1 if BTC close_(t-1) < SMA60_(t-1).
House regime rule using only the previous close and its 60-close average. Ties unclassified; window and state version stored.
interpretation:
ADA may appear inexplicably weak, but defensive-state exposure explains part of the
difference. The regime label does not predict when weakness ends.

name: Lagged Beta
description:
Investigate whether the response arrives
late
Lagged beta relates today's asset return to an earlier BTC return. It tests delayed association,
which can also arise from stale prices or misaligned clocks.
method:
r_i,t = α + β_k r_m,t-k + e_t; lagged_β(k)=β_k.
Single-lag OLS with intercept; k is explicit in metadata.
interpretation:
The chart suggests a leader-follower pattern. Most of the ATOM return still requires another
explanation, and clock alignment can erase the apparent lag.

name: Adjusted Beta
description:
Shrink a noisy estimate without hiding it
Adjusted beta pulls a raw estimate toward a reference value. The 0.67/0.33 convention is a
stability transform inherited from equity practice, not an empirically guaranteed crypto rule.
method:
β_adj = 0.67*β_raw + 0.33*1.00.
Blume-style shrinkage convention. We use it only as a stability transform, not as a crypto law.
interpretation:
A calmer adjusted number is not evidence that SEI became safer. It expresses a prior belief
about noisy estimates.

name: Beta Stability
description:
Ask whether the reaction estimate is
dependable
Beta stability measures how much estimated sensitivity varies across review dates. Lower
variability improves interpretability, but stability in one regime cannot guarantee stability in
the next.
method:
BetaStabilityRisk = SD({β_t(W)}) across evaluation dates; lower is more stable.
House diagnostic: sample SD of 60-observation rolling betas over the review interval.
interpretation:
The average looks moderate. The sequence suggests rising market sensitivity, so the latest
estimate and its uncertainty deserve more weight in review.

name: Covariance
description:
Measure the shared movement before
normalizing it
Covariance records whether two return series deviate from their averages together. Its units
are squared returns; the magnitude changes when percentages replace decimal returns.
method:
s_xy = sum[(x_t-x_bar)(y_t-y_bar)]/(n-1).
Unbiased sample covariance convention.
interpretation:
The three sessions show strong shared direction. Such a tiny demonstration sample explains
arithmetic, not estimation reliability.

name: Pearson Correlation
description:
Quantify how closely the asset follows
the anchor
Pearson correlation measures linear co-movement on a scale from -1 to +1. It normalizes
covariance but says nothing by itself about how large the asset's moves are.
method:
ρ_hat = sum[(x-x_bar)(y-y_bar)] / sqrt(sum[(x-x_bar)^2] sum[(y-y_bar)^2]).
Pearson product-moment correlation.
interpretation:
A high correlation supports a shared-market interpretation. It does not guarantee matching
returns on every day or protection during a tail event.

name: Spearman Rank Correlation
description:
Check whether the relationship survives
extreme values
Spearman correlation compares return ranks. It captures monotonic association with less
sensitivity to the size of extreme observations, while discarding economically important
magnitude information.
method:
ρ_s = Corr(rank(x), rank(y)); with no ties, ρ_s = 1 - 6*sum(d_i^2)/[n(n^2-1)].
Average ranks for ties; Pearson correlation of ranks is implementation convention.
interpretation:
UNI often preserves the ordering of BTC's stronger and weaker days. That observation does
not quantify a hedge ratio or the cost of an extreme token event.

name: Kendall Tau
description:
Count how often the ordering agrees
Kendall tau measures concordant versus discordant observation pairs. Its tie-adjusted form is
useful when data contain repeated values, but it is not numerically interchangeable with
Pearson correlation.
method:
τ_b = (C-D) / sqrt[(C+D+T_x)(C+D+T_y)].
Kendall tau-b, tie-adjusted.
interpretation:
FIL broadly follows BTC's ordering in this sample, although its biggest loss could still be much
larger than BTC's.

name: Rolling Correlation
description:
Detect when diversification begins to
disappear
Rolling correlation follows changes in shared direction. A rise can reveal market-wide stress,
but the estimate also depends on the volatility and event mix inside the window.
method:
ρ_t(W)=Corr(r_i,r_m) over t-W+1,...,t.
Trailing Pearson rolling correlation; W stored explicitly.
interpretation:
Holding different tickers may look diversified. Rising common movement means the basket
can behave increasingly like one risk position.

name: Cross Correlation
description:
Separate a genuine lead from a clock
mismatch
Cross-correlation measures association at specified positive and negative lags. The sign
convention here is Corr(asset at t, BTC at t-k), so positive k means BTC leads.
method:
ρ_xy(k)=Corr(x_t, y_{t-k}).
Cross-correlation at signed lag k; timestamps normalized before lagging.
interpretation:
A visually delayed response may be a data-delivery delay. Only a relationship that survives
timestamp repair and later testing merits further research.

name: Partial Correlation
description:
Remove BTC before calling two alts
connected
Partial correlation asks whether two assets remain related after controlling for a shared factor.
It can weaken a misleading peer narrative, but it removes only the modeled linear common
component.
method:
ρ_xy.z = (ρ_xy-ρ_xz*ρ_yz) / sqrt[(1-ρ_xz^2)(1-ρ_yz^2)].
First-order partial correlation controlling one factor z; matrix method used for >1 controls.
interpretation:
The chart suggests a tight sector pair. Most of that relationship may be BTC exposure; the
remaining association needs its own economic explanation.

name: Alpha or Intercept
description:
Find the average return left after
exposure
An intercept is the fitted average return at zero benchmark return. In a raw-return model it is
not automatically investment skill, and it becomes CAPM-style alpha only with consistent
excess returns.
method:
α_hat = y_bar - β_hat*x_bar in single-factor OLS with intercept.
OLS intercept; for excess-return CAPM variants both y and x are excess returns.
interpretation:
STX appears to earn return beyond its BTC exposure. The estimate describes this sample;
persistent edge requires forward evidence after costs.

name: R Squared
description:
Ask how much of the variation the model
explains
R-squared compares model error with total variation around the asset's mean. It evaluates
in-sample fit, not the probability that the next forecast is correct.
method:
R^2 = 1 - SSE/SST, where SSE=sum(e_t^2), SST=sum[(y_t-y_bar)^2].
OLS with intercept.
interpretation:
The model explains 70% of sample variation. It does not establish that 70% of today's move
was caused by BTC.

name: Adjusted R Squared
description:
Make extra factors earn their place
Adjusted R-squared penalizes adding regressors to an in-sample model. It is a useful
diagnostic, but only future-data evaluation can show whether complexity improves practical
performance.
method:
AdjR^2 = 1 - (1-R^2)*(n-1)/(n-k-1), k=number of regressors excluding intercept.
Standard adjusted R-squared.
interpretation:
A more elaborate explanation may fit better merely because it has more parameters. The
penalty encourages restraint but does not eliminate selection bias.

name: Residual
description:
Investigate what the market model
cannot explain
A residual is actual return minus fitted return. For live research, compute it using a model
fitted before the observation; otherwise it is an in-sample description.
method:
e_t = y_t - y_hat_t.
OLS residual using fitted values from the specified model.
interpretation:
The excess move is real relative to this model. Calling it organic demand requires evidence
beyond the residual itself.

name: Residual Volatility
description:
Measure the risk that a BTC hedge leaves
behind
Residual volatility measures the dispersion of returns not captured by the factor model. A
high-beta hedge can still leave large token-specific fluctuations.
method:
σ_e = SD(e_t); annualized residual volatility = σ_e*sqrt(A).
Sample SD of residuals, A=365 for non-overlapping UTC daily crypto returns.
interpretation:
A hedged basket may look market-neutral while remaining highly volatile. Residual risk must
receive a separate risk budget.

name: Standard Error of Beta
description:
Put uncertainty around the sensitivity
estimate
The standard error measures sampling uncertainty in a coefficient. The classical formula is a
reference case; dependence and changing volatility require robust covariance estimation.
method:
SE(β_hat) = sqrt[s_e^2 / sum(x_t-x_bar)^2], with s_e^2=SSE/(n-2), for classical
homoskedastic OLS.
Classical reference formula; production inference replaces this with HAC/Newey-West when residual dependence is present.
interpretation:
A clean fitted line can conceal clustered errors. The wider HAC uncertainty may be more
appropriate than the reassuring classical band.

name: T Statistic
description:
Test a specific exposure claim
A coefficient test compares an estimate with an explicit null value. Testing beta against zero
answers whether exposure exists; testing against one asks whether sensitivity differs from
BTC-like exposure.
method:
t = (β_hat-β_0)/SE(β_hat); common null β_0=0.
Two-sided OLS coefficient test; production uses HAC SE where required.
interpretation:
Evidence that XMR has market exposure is much stronger than evidence that its exposure
exceeds one. A single unlabeled statistic obscures that distinction.

name: P Value
description:
Read statistical surprise without
inventing certainty
A p-value is the probability, under the specified null and reference model, of a statistic at least
as extreme as observed. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
method:
Classical: p = 2[1 - F_t(|t|; n-k-1)].
Large-sample HAC convention here: p = 2[1 - Phi(|z|)].
The case uses the asymptotic normal reference; an exact finite-sample Student-t claim is reserved for the classical model.
interpretation:
A small p-value says the result is unusual under a model. It does not establish a profitable
strategy, a causal driver or a 98.36% chance of being right.

name: Confidence Interval
description:
Replace a point estimate with a plausible
range
A confidence interval makes estimation uncertainty visible. Its coverage interpretation
concerns repeated samples under model assumptions, not the probability of a realized
next-day return.
method:
Classical CI = β_hat ± t_(1-a/2,n-k-1) SE.
HAC asymptotic CI = β_hat ± z_(1-a/2) SE_HAC.
The example uses a 95% normal-reference HAC interval. Model and regime uncertainty are additional, not captured
automatically.
interpretation:
The point estimate looks exact on a dashboard. The interval reveals that materially different
hedge sizes remain compatible with the sample.

name: RMSE
description:
Penalize large forecasting mistakes
explicitly
Root mean squared error measures typical squared forecast error in return units. Its stronger
penalty on large misses makes it relevant when occasional severe errors dominate risk.
method:
RMSE = sqrt[(1/n)*sum(e_t^2)].
In-sample residual RMSE unless explicitly evaluated out-of-sample.
interpretation:
An articulate factor story can still be too imprecise for the proposed decision. Forecast scale
matters as much as fit.

name: MAE
description:
Measure the ordinary miss without
squaring it
Mean absolute error averages error magnitudes. It is easier to interpret than squared loss and
less dominated by one extreme miss, but it can underemphasize tail damage.
method:
MAE = (1/n)*sum|e_t|.
Mean absolute error on the stated evaluation sample.
interpretation:
A tolerable average absolute miss can coexist with an economically damaging outlier. Separate
routine forecast quality from stress performance.

name: Simple Return
description:
Start with the return an investor actually
experiences
Simple return measures proportional price change. It is the natural building block for cash
portfolio returns when adjusted prices and any distributions are handled consistently.
method:
R_t = P_t/P_(t-1) - 1.
Close-to-close simple return on a defined UTC boundary.
interpretation:
The strongest percentage move is not necessarily independent strength. The next step is to
compare SOL's return with its pre-estimated BTC exposure.

name: Log Return
description:
Use additive returns for multi-period
analysis
Log return is the logarithm of the price ratio. It adds through time for one asset, but portfolio
log return is not generally the weighted average of constituent log returns.
method:
r_t = ln(P_t/P_(t-1)).
Continuously compounded/log return.
interpretation:
A difference between simple and log returns is not a data contradiction. It grows as moves
become larger.

name: Cumulative Return
description:
Follow the wealth path through gains
and losses
Cumulative return compounds the sequence of simple returns. The order affects the drawdown
path even when the final product is unchanged.
method:
R_cum = product_t(1+R_t)-1.
Geometrically linked simple returns.
interpretation:
LINK still outperforms, but much less than a casual addition suggests. Evaluate the path and
the final wealth separately.

name: Mean Return
description:
Do not confuse an average day with
compounded growth
Arithmetic mean return summarizes the average one-period outcome. It is useful in
expected-return models but can overstate sustainable growth when returns are volatile.
method:
R_bar = (1/n)*sum R_t.
Arithmetic sample mean.
interpretation:
Positive average returns can be economically weak after volatility drag, fees and estimation
error. A short average is particularly fragile.

name: Median Return
description:
Describe the typical session when one
event dominates
The median is the middle ordered observation. It resists extreme values but cannot describe
the entire payoff distribution or replace the mean in every portfolio calculation.
method:
Median = 50th percentile of ordered returns.
Sample median with conventional midpoint interpolation for even n.
interpretation:
The apparent consistency disappears when typical and average outcomes are separated. The
12% event still matters for wealth and risk.

name: Variance
description:
Measure dispersion in squared-return
units
Variance measures average squared deviations using a stated denominator. It is central to
covariance models, although standard deviation is easier to read in return units.
method:
s^2 = sum(R_t-R_bar)^2/(n-1).
Unbiased sample variance.
interpretation:
A higher variance means more dispersed outcomes in this window. It does not distinguish
upside excitement from downside harm.

name: Standard Deviation
description:
Bring risk back into percentage-return
units
Standard deviation is the square root of variance. It summarizes dispersion around the mean
but does not imply that a normal distribution describes the tails.
method:
s = sqrt[s^2].
Sample standard deviation.
interpretation:
A quiet daily candle does not erase a volatile return history. Standard deviation measures the
broader sample, while a tail model asks a different question.

name: Annualized Volatility
description:
Annualize without changing the
underlying evidence
Annualized volatility rescales periodic standard deviation under a variance-scaling
assumption. The square-root rule is a convention, not a forecast guarantee under serial
dependence or changing regimes.
method:
σ_ann = σ_period*sqrt(A).
Square-root-of-time annualization; A=365 for non-overlapping daily crypto returns.
interpretation:
Annualized values are comparable only when return sampling and scaling match.
Weekday-only macro models require their own clock.

name: Realized Volatility
description:
Recover the movement hidden inside a
quiet close
Realized volatility aggregates squared intraday log returns. A small close-to-close return can
coexist with large intraday movement, which matters for execution and leveraged positions.
method:
RV_day = sqrt(sum_j log(P_j/P_(j-1))^2).
Multi-day annualized RV = sqrt[365 x mean_d(RV_day^2)].
Intraday log-return realized variance. One-day annualization is sqrt(365) times daily RV; multi-day estimates average variance
before taking the root.
interpretation:
The close shows no net move. The path shows meaningful risk and potential stop-outs, with
neither bullish nor bearish conviction implied.

name: EWMA Volatility
description:
Let recent shocks influence the volatility
estimate
EWMA gives declining weight to older squared returns. Its responsiveness is controlled by
lambda; the legacy 0.94 daily choice is explicit here so results can be reproduced.
method:
σ_t^2 = λ*σ_(t-1)^2 + (1-λ)*r_(t-1)^2.
RiskMetrics EWMA daily convention; lambda=0.94 is retained as a named legacy convention, not a crypto threshold.
interpretation:
A rising forecast reflects recent information, not advance knowledge of the next loss. EWMA
can lag a sudden change.

name: Downside Deviation
description:
Measure shortfalls relative to a declared
target
Downside deviation measures returns below a minimum acceptable return, using all
observations in the denominator. The target is an input to the analysis, not a universal
definition of a bad day.
method:
DownsideDev(MAR)=sqrt[(1/n)*sum min(0,R_t-MAR)^2]. Annualize by sqrt(A).
Target/MAR=0 in examples unless strategy mandate specifies another target.
interpretation:
The current gain can coexist with substantial downside variability. The target and observation
frequency must accompany the number.

name: Semivariance
description:
Keep the downside risk in variance form
Zero-target semivariance is the squared downside deviation under the same convention. It
distinguishes harmful variation from upside movements but still ignores path and liquidity.
method:
Semivariance_0 = (1/n)*sum min(0,R_t)^2.
Zero-target lower semivariance.
interpretation:
Positive days do not cancel squared shortfalls. The metric separates favorable volatility from
the losses that consume a downside budget.

name: Skewness
description:
Look for a distribution tilted toward
severe losses
Moment skewness measures distributional asymmetry. Negative skew often means the left tail
is longer, but a few observations can make the estimate unstable.
method:
g1 = m3 / m2^(3/2), where mk=(1/n)*sum(R-R_bar)^k.
Moment skewness (unadjusted Fisher-Pearson moment coefficient); bias-corrected software values may differ.
interpretation:
Frequent small gains may conceal infrequent large losses. Negative sample skew is a warning
about payoff shape, not a precise forecast of the next crash.

name: Kurtosis
description:
Identify tails that a normal model may
understate
Excess kurtosis compares the fourth standardized moment with the normal benchmark of
three. It is sensitive to extreme observations and should not be interpreted as a simple measure
of peak height.
method:
ExcessKurtosis = m4/m2^2 - 3.
Fisher excess-kurtosis moment convention; Pearson kurtosis would omit -3.
interpretation:
The market may look quiet between bursts. A large fourth moment records how much the
extremes dominate the distribution.

name: Drawdown
description:
Measure how far capital sits below its
previous peak
Drawdown compares current marked wealth with its running high. It captures the path
experienced by an investor, unlike a one-period volatility statistic.
method:
DD_t = V_t / max_(s<=t)V_s - 1.
Peak-to-current percentage drawdown on a marked-to-market wealth index.
interpretation:
A strong rebound can still leave the position deeply underwater. Evaluate recovery relative to
the prior peak, not only yesterday's close.

name: Maximum Drawdown
description:
Locate the deepest capital impairment
Maximum drawdown is the worst peak-to-trough decline in the observation window. It is
path-dependent and sample-specific, not a future maximum loss promise.
method:
MDD = min_t DD_t; reported loss magnitude is |MDD|.
Maximum peak-to-trough drawdown over the stated sample.
interpretation:
An end-to-end return can hide a much more difficult investor experience. The interim peak
changes the risk story.

name: Recovery Time
description:
Measure the time capital remains
underwater
Recovery time measures duration from a prior peak to its first full recovery. A position that has
not recovered has a censored duration, not a completed recovery time.
method:
RecoveryTime = t_recovery - t_peak, where V_t_recovery >= V_t_peak after the
drawdown.
Peak-to-full-recovery duration convention.
interpretation:
A rebound narrative omits the opportunity cost of immobilized capital. Both depth and
duration belong in the review.

name: Sharpe Ratio
description:
Evaluate excess return per unit of
ordinary risk
The Sharpe ratio divides mean excess return by its standard deviation. It is highly sensitive to
expected-return estimation and can look strong for strategies with hidden tail losses.
method:
Sharpe = (mean(R_p-R_f)/SD(R_p-R_f))*sqrt(A).
Arithmetic mean excess return divided by sample SD; A=365 for daily crypto observations.
interpretation:
A positive ratio indicates favorable historical reward relative to dispersion. It says little about
the reliability of the estimated mean or the worst liquidation path.

name: Sortino Ratio
description:
Judge reward against harmful variability
Sortino compares mean return above a target with downside deviation. It focuses the
denominator on shortfalls, which makes the target and negative-observation count essential
context.
method:
Sortino = [mean(R_p-MAR)*A] / DownsideDev_ann(MAR).
MAR=0 in the stated case; downside deviation uses all n observations.
interpretation:
The payoff looks favorable relative to observed shortfalls. Sparse loss observations do not
establish that downside risk is structurally small.

name: Calmar Ratio
description:
Compare growth with the worst observed
drawdown
Calmar relates annualized geometric growth to maximum drawdown magnitude. It links
return to path damage, but both quantities depend heavily on the chosen start and end dates.
method:
CAGR = (V_end/V_start)^(365/calendar_days) - 1.
Calmar = CAGR / |MDD|.
Geometric annualized return and maximum drawdown from the same wealth path and evaluation window.
interpretation:
The strategy earned growth at the cost of a substantial interim loss. Neither quantity should be
cherry-picked from different windows.

name: Treynor Ratio
description:
Separate reward for market exposure
from total risk
Treynor divides annual excess return by beta. It evaluates reward per unit of systematic
exposure and is inappropriate as a complete risk measure for a concentrated altcoin position.
method:
Treynor = (R_p-R_f) / β_p,m.
Annualized excess return divided by market beta.
interpretation:
The market-exposure reward looks adequate in isolation. Token-specific risk and liquidity
remain outside the denominator.

name: Jensen Alpha
description:
Audit return beyond the excess-return
model
Jensen alpha is the intercept in an excess-return regression. Arithmetic annualization is a
reporting approximation, not the compounded wealth generated by an investable alpha
stream.
method:
R_p,t - R_f,t = α + β(R_BTC,t - R_f,t) + e_t.
α_hat = mean(R_p-R_f) - β_hat mean(R_BTC-R_f).
JensenAlpha_ann = 365 x α_daily.
Jensen-style excess-return OLS with BTC as the declared crypto benchmark. Arithmetic annualization is an approximation; it is
not a claim that BTC is the theoretical CAPM market portfolio.
interpretation:
A positive point estimate may disappear after uncertainty and unmodeled exposures are
considered. Excess-return inputs must match the financing convention.

name: Information Ratio
description:
Measure the quality of returns beyond a
benchmark
Information ratio measures mean active return relative to active-return volatility. It rewards
consistent benchmark outperformance, not merely a high absolute return.
method:
IR = mean(R_p-R_b)/SD(R_p-R_b)*sqrt(A).
Information ratio on synchronous active returns.
interpretation:
The basket adds a modest amount of return relative to its benchmark deviations. A high-beta
strategy can still owe much of this to the sample regime.

name: Tracking Error
description:
Quantify how differently the portfolio
behaves
Tracking error is the volatility of active returns. It measures benchmark deviation, which may
reflect intentional positioning or uncontrolled exposure rather than poor performance.
method:
TrackingError = SD(R_p-R_b)*sqrt(A).
Annualized SD of active returns.
interpretation:
A less volatile portfolio can still deviate substantially from BTC. Tracking error and total
volatility answer different questions.

name: Upside Capture
description:
Evaluate participation during
benchmark gains
Upside capture compares geometric mean returns on periods when the benchmark rises. It
describes conditional compounded participation and is distinct from an upside regression
slope.
method:
UpsideCapture = [GM(R_p | R_b>0) / GM(R_b | R_b>0)]*100, GM=geometric mean period
return.
Conditional geometric capture convention; benchmark-positive periods only.
interpretation:
PENDLE amplified positive benchmark periods. The price of that amplification appears only
when downside periods and risk are also examined.

name: Downside Capture
description:
Assess participation in the benchmark's
losses
Downside capture compares conditional geometric returns when the benchmark falls. When
both returns are negative, a ratio above 100% means deeper loss participation.
method:
DownsideCapture = [GM(R_p | R_b<0) / GM(R_b | R_b<0)]*100.
Conditional geometric capture on benchmark-negative periods.
interpretation:
ICP historically lost roughly one-and-a-half times the benchmark's conditional geometric
return in this small demonstration. That is descriptive, not a downside cap.

name: Historical VaR
description:
Locate the empirical loss threshold
Historical VaR is a quantile of realized losses over a specified horizon. It describes a threshold
exceeded with a chosen tail probability under the empirical distribution, not the largest
possible loss.
method:
Sort losses L_(1) <= ... <= L_(n). h=(n-1)q.
VaR_q = L_(floor(h)+1) + (h-floor(h))[L_(ceil(h)+1)-L_(floor(h)+1)].
Linear empirical quantile, with one-based ordered losses and zero-based interpolation coordinate h. Loss L=-R.
interpretation:
Today's loss is inside the historical threshold. That does not certify safety, especially when the
sample contains only one observation in the upper 10%.

name: Parametric VaR
description:
See what the normal-loss assumption
buys and misses
Gaussian parametric VaR converts a mean and standard deviation into a loss quantile. Its
convenience depends on a distributional assumption that crypto tails often violate.
method:
NormalVaR_q = z_q*σ_R - μ_R for loss L=-R.
Gaussian parametric one-period VaR; z_q is standard-normal quantile.
interpretation:
A smooth normal curve may show manageable risk while jumps and fat tails create much
larger losses.

name: Monte Carlo VaR
description:
Simulate the portfolio rather than just its
headline price
Monte Carlo VaR is a quantile of simulated, repriced losses. The simulation is only as credible
as its dependence, volatility, jump, liquidity and instrument assumptions.
method:
Siμlate joint risk factors, fully reprice each scenario to obtain L_s.
For the stated case: VaR_q = L_(ceil(qS)) after sorting S losses.
Nearest-rank empirical quantile for the Monte Carlo case; differs deliberately from the linear historical quantile in metric 60.
Model, seed and units are recorded.
interpretation:
A large simulation count reduces numerical sampling noise. It does not cure a model that
excludes the event that matters.

name: CVaR or Expected Shortfall
description:
Estimate the loss after the threshold is
breached
Expected shortfall averages the worst specified fraction of loss probability. It asks how severe
the tail is after VaR, with careful treatment of discrete samples and ties.
method:
ES_q = [1/(1-q)] integral_q^1 VaR_u du.
For continuous distributions: ES_q = E[L | L >= VaR_q].
For empirical distributions, integrate the inverse empirical CDF with fractional weight at the tail boundary. The case has an
exact integer tail count.
interpretation: VaR marks the entrance to the tail; ES describes its average severity. Neither is a hard loss cap.

name: Stress Test
description:
Revalue the book under a coherent shock
A stress test applies a specified adverse scenario to positions. It is a conditional damage
estimate, not a statement that the scenario has a known probability.
method:
StressPnL = sum_i w_i * (P_i^stress/P_i - 1) for linear spot holdings; derivatives
require full repricing.
Deterministic scenario revaluation, not a probability statement.
interpretation:
A diversified-looking allocation can suffer jointly when liquidity withdraws. The weakest
executable market may dominate the practical loss.

name: Scenario Analysis
description:
Compare mechanisms before choosing
one narrative
Scenario analysis evaluates multiple internally consistent states. It is especially useful when
several explanations fit today's evidence and their future paths differ.
method:
ScenarioPnL_s = V(x+Δ x_s)/V(x)-1, evaluated for every scenario s.
Full-revaluation scenario set; report worst, median and component contributions without assigning fake probabilities.
interpretation:
The current chart may support one confident story. A scenario set preserves credible
alternatives and exposes the consequences of being wrong.

name: Ulcer Index
description:
Combine drawdown depth and
persistence
The Ulcer Index is the root mean square of percentage drawdowns. Repeated underwater
observations increase it even when the maximum drawdown does not change.
method:
UlcerIndex = sqrt[(1/n)*sum(D_t^2)], with D_t expressed as percentage drawdown from
prior peak.
Percentage-point drawdown convention.
interpretation:
The latest rebound looks encouraging, yet repeated time below the peak remains part of the
investor's experience.

name: Omega Ratio
description:
Compare total gains and shortfalls
around a target
Omega compares the sum of returns above a target with the sum of shortfalls below it. The
complete empirical distribution enters, but the result is highly target-dependent.
method:
Omega(τ)=sum max(R_t-τ,0) / sum max(τ-R_t,0) in the empirical sample.
Empirical Omega; tau=0 in the example.
interpretation:
The payoff looks attractive relative to zero but weak relative to a demanding target. Neither
reading is meaningful without naming that target.

name: Autocorrelation
description:
Test whether returns retain a short
memory
Autocorrelation relates an asset's returns to its own lagged returns. A nonzero estimate can
reflect genuine dynamics, stale data, microstructure or overlapping measurement.
method:
ρ_k = Corr(R_t, R_(t-k)).
Sample Pearson autocorrelation at lag k.
interpretation:
The series shows modest persistence in the sample. That association may vanish after latency,
spread and costs are included.

name: ACF
description:
Read the entire lag pattern rather than
one bar
The autocorrelation function presents dependence over multiple lags using one stated
estimator. It helps distinguish isolated lag effects from a persistent decay pattern.
method:
ACF(k)=γ(k)/γ(0), γ(k)=(1/n)*sum_(t=k+1..n)(R_t-R_bar)(R_(t-k)-R_bar).
Biased-denominator ACF convention consistent across lags for display.
interpretation:
A visible ACF bar is a diagnostic clue. A four-point illustration cannot support an economic
claim of predictability.

name: PACF
description:
Remove intermediate lags before
crediting a distant one
Partial autocorrelation at lag k measures the final lag coefficient in a projection on lags one
through k. It isolates incremental linear dependence after the intervening lags.
method:
PACF(k)=φ_(k,k), the coefficient on R_(t-k) in the linear projection of R_t on lags
1..k.
Yule-Walker/linear-projection definition; implementation method recorded.
interpretation:
A second ACF bar does not necessarily imply a second independent predictive channel. The
shorter lag may carry the entire linear relation.

name: Stationarity
description:
Ask whether one statistical description
remains credible
Weak stationarity requires a constant mean, finite constant variance and lag-dependent
covariance. It is a property of a process, not a single numerical score.
method:
Weak stationarity requires E[X_t]=μ constant, Var[X_t]=γ(0) finite/constant, and
Cov(X_t,X_(t- k))=γ(k) dependent only on lag k.
Definition, not a single test statistic; operational checks use ADF plus KPSS and rolling moments.
interpretation:
A chart can appear to oscillate around a moving level while the process itself has changed.
Statistical assumptions require testing and economic review.

name: ADF Test
description:
Test the unit-root hypothesis explicitly
The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test evaluates a unit-root null using a regression with lagged
differences. Its statistic has a nonstandard reference distribution determined by the
specification.
method:
Δ y_t = a + γ y_(t-1) + sum_(j=1..p) d_j Δ y_(t-j) + e_t.
ADF statistic = γ_hat / SE(γ_hat); H0: γ=0.
Intercept-only ADF convention here, lag selection recorded. A trend term is a different specification with different critical
values.
interpretation:
Rejection supports mean-reversion research under the model. Breaks, costs and hedge
instability can still make the apparent opportunity unusable.

name: KPSS Test
description:
Challenge stationarity from the opposite
direction
KPSS starts with a stationarity null. Used alongside ADF, it helps identify cases where the data
are consistent, contradictory or simply too weak to support a firm conclusion.
method:
KPSS statistic = [sum_(t=1..T) S_t^2] / [T^2 * s_LR^2], S_t=cuμlative residuals from
deterministic component. H0: stationarity.
KPSS level-stationary or trend-stationary specification is explicit; long-run variance estimator recorded.
interpretation:
The test does not prove stationarity. A near-boundary result is especially sensitive to
bandwidth, sample and deterministic terms.

name: Z Score
description:
Measure surprise relative to a past
baseline
A z-score expresses a deviation in baseline standard-deviation units. For an alert, the baseline
here excludes the current observation so the event cannot dilute its own surprise.
method:
z_t = [x_t - mean(x_(t-W),...,x_(t-1))] / SD(x_(t-W),...,x_(t-1)).
House alert convention excludes the current observation. Sample SD uses W-1. Zero baseline variance yields unavailable, not
infinity.
interpretation:
The move is unusual relative to recent modeled behavior. Its sign does not tell whether
informed repricing will continue or a squeeze will fade.

name: Cointegration
description:
Test a shared long-run relationship
without confusing it with correlation
Cointegration means nonstationary series share a stationary linear combination. High return
correlation alone is insufficient, and the economic basis of the relationship must be defensible.
method:
Engle-Granger: y_t = a + b*x_t + e_t; series are cointegrated if residual e_t is
stationary under a residual unit-root test.
Two-step Engle-Granger with documented deterministic terms and lag selection.
interpretation:
A temporary divergence may be a spread deviation or a permanent structural break. The
statistical test cannot supply a missing economic anchor.

name: Half Life of Mean Reversion
description:
Estimate how quickly a deviation might
decay
AR(1) half-life converts a stable persistence coefficient into the time needed for expected
deviation magnitude to halve. It assumes the fitted dynamics remain valid.
method:
x_t = c + φ x_(t-1) + e_t.
For 0<|φ|<1, magnitude half-life = ln(0.5)/ln(|φ|).
Positive phi gives monotone expected decay; negative phi alternates sign. phi=0 decays in one step; |phi|>=1 does not
support stable decay.
interpretation:
The estimate describes expected decay, not a deadline by which the trade must recover.
Liquidity and model failure can dominate the path.

name: Granger Causality Test
description:
Test incremental forecasting content
without claiming causation
A Granger test asks whether lagged BTC returns improve prediction of an asset beyond its own
lags. The word causality refers to a forecasting definition, not economic proof of cause.
method:
F = [(SSR_R-SSR_U)/m] / [SSR_U/(T-k_U)] comparing restricted y-lag model vs
unrestricted model adding m lags of x.
Linear Granger causality F-test; lag order chosen before inference.
interpretation:
Lagged BTC contains incremental in-sample information under this model. Shared news,
timestamp problems and omitted factors can still explain it.

name: Hurst Exponent
description:
Investigate persistence across several
scales
The Hurst exponent summarizes scaling in a specified process and estimator. Classical
rescaled-range estimates are sensitive to short samples, trends and short-run dependence.
method:
Y_k = sum_(j=1..k)(x_j - mean(x_1,...,x_n)).
R(n)=max(Y_1,...,Y_n)-min(Y_1,...,Y_n); S(n)=population SD(x_1,...,x_n).
H = OLS slope of ln(mean_block[R(n)/S(n)]) on ln(n).
Classical rescaled-range convention, with non-overlapping blocks at predeclared sizes and zero-variance blocks excluded.
Finite samples and short-memory effects can bias the estimate.
interpretation:
The scaling pattern suggests persistence in this constructed sample. A trend, volatility
clustering or finite-sample bias may produce a similar estimate.

name: GARCH Style Conditional Volatility
description:
Model volatility as a changing state
GARCH forecasts conditional variance from prior shocks and prior variance. It models
volatility clustering, not the sign of the next return.
method:
σ_t^2 = ω + a e_(t-1)^2 + b σ_(t-1)^2.
ω>0; a,b>=0; a+b<1 for covariance-stationary finite-variance specification.
GARCH(1,1), with Gaussian or variance-standardized Student-t innovations; distribution and parameter-estimation window
recorded.
interpretation:
A falling token can enter a high-volatility state without the model predicting another fall.
Innovation distribution and persistence remain crucial.

name: Change Point Detection
description:
Recognize when yesterday's baseline
stops fitting
CUSUM accumulates small departures from a fixed reference mean. A signal indicates a
potential shift requiring investigation, with false-alarm behavior determined by its calibration.
method:
C_t+ = max[0, C_(t-1)+ + x_t - μ0 - k].
C_t- = min[0, C_(t-1)- + x_t - μ0 + k]. Alert if C_t+>h or C_t-<-h.
Two-sided tabular CUSUM on a declared standardized baseline. k and h are calibration parameters, not universal crypto
thresholds.
interpretation:
The apparent series of ordinary gains may represent a persistent change in residual behavior.
It could be a new regime or a feed problem.

name: Trading Volume
description:
Count executed activity without
assigning conviction
Trading volume sums executed notional over a declared instrument and venue universe. Every
trade has a buyer and seller; high volume alone does not identify who initiated it or why.
method:
DollarVolume_T = sum_j Price_j * Quantity_j over executed trades j in interval T.
Executed-trade notional; venue and instrument universe explicit.
interpretation:
The burst establishes activity. It may represent directional demand, arbitrage, forced covering
or repeated turnover of the same inventory.

name: Turnover
description:
Relate activity to the size of the
circulating asset
Turnover scales spot traded notional by circulating market capitalization. It measures activity
relative to asset size, not the fraction of distinct investors who traded.
method:
Turnover_T = DollarVolume_T / MarketCap_T.
Spot-equivalent dollar volume divided by circulating market cap; derivatives excluded unless separately labeled.
interpretation:
High turnover looks like broad participation but can arise from concentrated speculation or
mechanical market making.

name: Bid Ask Spread
description:
Read the immediate cost of crossing the
market
Quoted spread measures the gap between best bid and ask relative to their midpoint. It is the
visible first layer of execution cost, before depth, market impact and fees.
method:
QuotedSpread_bps = (BestAsk-BestBid)/Mid * 10,000, Mid=(Ask+Bid)/2.
Top-of-book quoted spread immediately before observation/trade.
interpretation:
A modest price move can hide deteriorating tradability. A narrow spread on one venue does
not establish deep liquidity across the market.

name: Market Depth
description:
Measure executable-looking depth on
both sides
Market depth sums displayed size within a fixed distance from mid, separately for bids and
asks. It describes available intent at the observation time, not guaranteed fills.
method:
Depth_bps(b) = sum quote notional with bid prices >= Mid*(1-b/10000) plus ask side
separately within symmetric band.
Report bid and ask depth separately at a declared band b; example b=10 bps.
interpretation:
The snapshot shows a stronger bid side. Cancellation behavior can invalidate the apparent
support before it becomes executed evidence.

name: Slippage
description:
Measure the gap between the decision
and the fill
Slippage compares execution VWAP with the pre-trade midpoint, signed so adverse execution
is positive. Fees and financing should be shown separately from the price concession.
method:
Slippage_bps = side*(VWAP_exec-Mid_pre)/Mid_pre*10,000, side=+1 buy, -1 sell.
Decision/pre-trade mid benchmark; include fees separately.
interpretation:
A correct directional call can still have poor economics. The executable price matters more
than the chart's mid-price return.

name: Price Impact
description:
Observe what the midpoint does after
aggressive flow
Post-trade impact measures signed midpoint change over a specified horizon. It captures price
response but is not automatically a causal estimate of the trade's effect.
method:
Impact_bps(h)=side*(Mid_(t+h)-Mid_t)/Mid_t*10,000 after a fixed horizon h.
Post-trade mid impact; horizon h versioned, e.g. 60 seconds for one report.
interpretation:
Aggressive buying visibly moved the quote, but much of the move did not persist. Persistence
adds information beyond volume.

name: Amihud Illiquidity
description:
Estimate price movement per dollar
traded
Amihud illiquidity averages absolute daily return divided by dollar volume. It is a coarse proxy
for price responsiveness to activity and should be compared only with consistent units.
method:
ILLIQ = (1/D)*sum_d |R_d| / DollarVolume_d.
Amihud daily illiquidity; report units or multiply by a documented scale factor for readability.
interpretation:
A high ratio flags a market where modest flow can accompany large movement. It does not
identify the initiator or prove manipulation.

name: Kyle Lambda
description:
Estimate how signed flow translates into
price response
An empirical Kyle-style slope relates midpoint changes to signed aggressive flow. The
estimated units depend on whether price changes are dollars, returns or basis points.
method:
ΔMid_t = α + λ*SignedFlow_t + e_t; KyleLambda=λ_hat.
Empirical Kyle-style price-impact regression using signed aggressive dollar flow and midpoint change.
interpretation:
Large buy flow with weak response can suggest absorption. It may also reflect arbitrage supply
or a changed liquidity state.

name: Order Book Imbalance
description:
Test whether the displayed book is
one-sided
Order-book imbalance compares bid and ask depth inside the same price band. It is a
normalized view of displayed intent, which can change faster than a strategy can respond.
method:
OBI = (BidDepth-AskDepth)/(BidDepth+AskDepth).
Symmetric depth band and venue fixed before calculation.
interpretation:
The visible book is bid-heavy at that instant. Durability, fills and replenishment determine
whether the support is economically meaningful.

name: Trade Imbalance
description:
Identify which side initiates execution
Trade imbalance compares buyer- and seller-initiated notional. It describes aggressor
pressure; every execution still has a counterparty on the passive side.
method:
TradeImbalance = (AggBuyNotional-AggSellNotional)/(AggBuyNotional+AggSellNotional).
Aggressor side from exchange flags or Lee-Ready-style inference when flags unavailable.
interpretation:
Buyers are more aggressive in the observed sample. Strong passive supply can absorb that
pressure without a sustained rise.

name: Cumulative Volume Delta
description:
Follow cumulative aggressive demand
through the episode
CVD accumulates buyer-initiated volume minus seller-initiated volume from a declared reset.
Its level depends on the starting point and its units must remain consistent.
method:
CVD_t = CVD_(t-1) + AggBuyVolume_t - AggSellVolume_t.
Cumulative aggressor-volume delta; reset convention and units are explicit.
interpretation:
A green CVD line supports net aggressive buying on the covered venues. It does not represent
all investors' net holdings or guarantee continuation.

name: VWAP
description:
Use an execution-weighted reference
price
VWAP averages trade prices weighted by quantity. It is a benchmark for activity over a defined
interval, not an intrinsic value or automatic support level.
method:
VWAP = sum_j P_j Q_j / sum_j Q_j.
Trade-volume-weighted average execution price in interval.
interpretation:
Trading above VWAP shows location relative to executed volume in this interval. Thin late
prints can create that appearance without broad participation.

name: Liquidity Stress Composite
description:
Combine liquidity warnings without
disguising judgment
The liquidity-stress composite averages standardized spread, slippage, impact and negative
depth. It is an explicit house diagnostic, not a calibrated probability of a trap.
method:
LiquidityStress = [z(Spread)+z(Slippage)+z(Impact)-z(Depth)]/4.
House equal-weight standardized composite; each z-score is trailing, venue-consistent and winsorization policy versioned.
interpretation:
The market may advertise a tradable breakout while execution conditions deteriorate. The
composite identifies the need for a size and data-quality review.

name: Open Interest
description:
Measure outstanding contracts without
inventing a direction
Open interest counts outstanding derivative contracts, normally once per matched long-short
pair. USD conversion must follow each contract's multiplier and settlement design.
method:
Linear OI_USD = open contracts x base-units per contract x mark USD.
Inverse fixed-USD contracts: OI_USD = open contracts x USD face value.
Count matched contracts once. Contract specification governs conversion; keep native exposure before summing normalized
instruments.
interpretation:
Large OI shows outstanding exposure and potential forced-flow capacity. It does not identify
the net directional conviction of the whole market.

name: OI Change
description:
Separate new positioning from
mark-price inflation
OI change measures the proportional change in outstanding exposure. In USD terms it
combines changes in contract count with changes in price, so native units are essential.
method:
ΔOI% = OI_t/OI_(t-1)-1.
Percent change in normalized OI.
interpretation:
Some apparent leverage growth is price appreciation. Remaining contract growth still matters,
but its direction requires other evidence.

name: OI to Market Cap
description:
Scale derivative exposure against the
circulating market
OI-to-market-cap places derivatives exposure in relation to circulating token value. It is a
rough pressure indicator, not a measurement of total leverage or available collateral.
method:
OI_to_MCap = AggregateOI_USD / CirculatingMarketCap_USD.
Same-timestamp aggregate derivative OI divided by circulating market cap.
interpretation:
The ratio makes exposure comparable in scale, while liquidation sensitivity still depends on
leverage distribution and liquidity.

name: Funding Rate
description:
Read the periodic price of leveraged
exposure
Funding transfers value between perpetual longs and shorts under venue-specific rules.
Positive funding commonly means longs pay shorts; the realized payment differs from an
indicative rate that can still change.
method:
F_base = [P + clamp(I-P, -0.05%, +0.05%)] x N/8.
F_final = clamp(F_base, contract floor, contract cap).
Binance-style rule updated September 2025: P is weighted average premium, I the 8-hour interest component, N interval
hours. Prefer realized published rates; contract exceptions apply.
interpretation:
Positive funding supports a crowding hypothesis but can persist alongside strong spot demand.
It does not time a reversal.

name: Annualized Funding
description:
Translate recurring funding into a stated
carry convention
Compounded annualization illustrates the scale of a periodic rate if it repeated and could be
reinvested. Actual funding cash flows generally follow changing rates and changing position
notionals.
method:
Funding_ann = (1+f_interval)^(24*365/h) - 1.
Compounded annualization for interval h hours; also report raw interval rate because annualized values explode during stress.
interpretation:
The annualized figure describes the current rate's scale. It does not establish a locked return or
a forecast of year-long funding.

name: Futures Basis
description:
Compare a dated future with its spot
anchor
Futures basis is the premium or discount of a dated future relative to matched spot or index. It
includes financing, positioning and frictions rather than a pure forecast of future spot price.
method:
Basis = F/S - 1.
Dated futures price F relative to contemporaneous spot/index S.
interpretation:
A futures premium can look bullish but may mainly compensate financing and balance-sheet
constraints. The spot purchase and futures hedge are separate execution problems.

name: Annualized Basis
description:
Normalize basis across different expiries
Annualized basis converts a dated premium into a common time scale. The compounded
convention used here differs from simple annualization, especially for large premiums or short
maturities.
method:
Basis_ann = (F/S)^(365/d) - 1, d=calendar days to expiry.
Compounded calendar-day annualization.
interpretation:
The annualized premium permits tenor comparison. It is not a free yield and can fluctuate
before convergence.

name: Liquidation Volume
description:
Separate forced liquidation from
voluntary conviction
Liquidation volume measures exchange-reported forced executions. Long liquidations
generally create selling pressure; short liquidations create buying pressure, subject to venue
mechanics and feed coverage.
method:
LiquidationVolume_T = sum_j |PositionNotional_j| for exchange-reported forced
liquidation executions during T.
Forced-execution notional; keep long-liquidation and short-liquidation sides separate.
interpretation:
The rise may contain a large forced-covering component. It could continue, but the liquidation
burst alone does not prove durable demand.

name: Liquidations to OI
description:
Put forced turnover in relation to open
exposure
Liquidation-to-OI scales forced executed notional by average outstanding exposure over the
same interval. It measures stress intensity under the chosen coverage, not the fraction of
investors liquidated.
method:
Liq_to_OI = LiquidationVolume_T / AverageOI_T.
Liquidation notional divided by average normalized OI over same interval.
interpretation:
A severe red candle may reflect positions being closed under compulsion. That is different from
a measured change in long-term investor beliefs.

name: Long Short Ratio
description:
Do not confuse account counts with
exposure size
An account long/short ratio counts classified accounts. It does not reveal their sizes and differs
from a position-notional ratio or a market-wide net exposure measure.
method:
AccountLongShortRatio = NumberOfLongAccounts / NumberOfShortAccounts.
Binance account-ratio convention; do not confuse with position-notional ratio.
interpretation:
More accounts lean long, but larger accounts may lean short in the selected sample. Neither
statistic describes all market participants.

name: Implied Volatility
description:
Infer the volatility embedded in option
prices
Implied volatility is the model input that reproduces an observed option premium. It is a price
of option uncertainty and protection, not a direct physical forecast.
method:
C = S exp(-qT) Phi(d1) - K exp(-rT) Phi(d2).
d1=[ln(S/K)+(r-q+σ^2/2)T]/(σ sqrt(T)); d2=d1-σ sqrt(T).
IV is the nonnegative σ solving C_model(σ)=C_market.
Dollar-settled European Black-Scholes-Merton convention for the case. Production uses the instrument's actual forward,
discounting and premium/settlement units.
interpretation:
The premium embeds substantial uncertainty. It can include insurance demand, supply
constraints and risk premium rather than a forecast of a 70% realized move.

name: IV Minus Realized Vol
description:
Compare the price of uncertainty with its
recent realization
IV minus realized volatility contrasts option-implied and historical realized annualized
volatility. The horizons are different by nature, so the spread is a diagnostic rather than a
guaranteed premium.
method:
IVminusRV = ATM_IV_ann - RealizedVol_ann.
Both expressed in annualized volatility points with matched horizon as closely as possible.
interpretation:
The options market prices more uncertainty than the recent path delivered. Future event risk
and risk premium are competing explanations.

name: Volatility Skew
description:
Read which side of the option surface is
expensive
The 25-delta risk reversal compares call and put implied volatility at matched expiry and delta
convention. This book uses call minus put, so a negative value indicates richer downside
volatility.
method:
RR25 = IV_25delta_call - IV_25delta_put.
25-delta risk-reversal sign convention used here. Some desks quote put-minus-call; sign conflict is explicitly flagged.
interpretation:
A negative skew documents the relative price of downside optionality. Positioning, structured
products and supply constraints can shape it.

name: Volatility Term Structure
description:
Locate where uncertainty sits along the
expiry curve
Volatility term structure compares implied volatility across maturities. Far-minus-near slope
highlights whether near-term events or longer-run uncertainty dominate the quoted surface.
method:
TermSlope = ATM_IV(T_far) - ATM_IV(T_near), in volatility points.
Far-minus-near convention; maturities are specified, no silent interpolation.
interpretation:
An inverted volatility curve often points to concentrated near-term uncertainty. It is not itself a
bearish price forecast.

name: Put Call Ratio
description:
Interpret put and call activity without
guessing its direction
Put/call ratio compares option volume or open interest under a declared convention. Volume
does not reveal whether options were bought or sold, nor whether trades form spreads.
method:
PutCallRatio_volume = PutOptionVolume / CallOptionVolume.
Volume-based PCR; open-interest PCR is a different metric and must be labeled separately.
interpretation:
Put activity dominates the count. The directional inference remains unresolved until trade
side, size, tenor and multi-leg structure are examined.

name: Exchange Inflow
description:
Treat an exchange deposit as potential
supply
Exchange inflow counts transfers entering a provider's labeled exchange boundary. It observes
settlement into an address cluster; it does not establish a sale on the exchange.
method:
Inflow_T = sum(value of transfers crossing from outside into labeled exchange
entities).
CryptoQuant exchange-flow convention selected for operational intake; use one frozen exchange universe and
provider-adjusted external transfers. Labels are estimates.
interpretation:
A large deposit can precede selling, collateral posting, custody changes or market-maker
inventory transfer. Only the transfer is confirmed.

name: Exchange Outflow
description:
Interpret withdrawals without declaring
accumulation
Exchange outflow measures transfers leaving a defined labeled exchange boundary. It can
indicate custody migration, collateral movement or other operational activity as well as
investment-related withdrawal.
method:
Outflow_T = sum(value of transfers crossing from labeled exchange entities to
outside).
CryptoQuant-style exchange boundary consistent with inflow; exclude internal transfers using the selected provider
convention and label version.
interpretation:
The withdrawal reduces the observed exchange balance. It does not prove a new spot purchase
or an unhedged bullish position.

name: Exchange Netflow
description:
Net the exchange boundary while
preserving both directions
Netflow subtracts outflow from inflow, with positive values indicating net deposits in this book.
Gross flows still matter because offsetting large movements can disappear in the net.
method:
ExchangeNetflow = Inflow - Outflow.
Positive means net flow into labeled exchanges in this manual.
interpretation:
Net deposits raise potential supply availability. Concentrated operational flows may explain
them without broad investor distribution.

name: Exchange Supply
description:
Measure the share held inside labeled
exchanges
Exchange supply share compares labeled exchange balances with circulating supply. It is a
custody-location measure and depends on the completeness of the labeling universe.
method:
ExchangeSupplyShare = ExchangeEntityBalance / CirculatingSupply.
Balance held by labeled exchange entities divided by circulating supply.
interpretation:
A declining ratio can appear bullish while simply reflecting circulating-supply growth. Balance
changes and classification changes must be separated.

name: Realized Capitalization
description:
Reconstruct the cost basis encoded in
coin movement
BTC realized capitalization values each current UTXO at the reference USD price when it was
created. It is a movement-based accounting proxy, not a record of actual purchase prices.
method:
BTC realized cap = sum_(u in current UTXOs) q_u x USD_price_at_creation(u).
Coin Metrics CapRealUSD chosen for the realized-cap family; BTC UTXO method. Account-based assets need their own
documented inventory accounting.
interpretation:
A gap between current and movement-based values suggests aggregate embedded gains in the
accounting model. Self-transfers and lost coins complicate the economic interpretation.

name: MVRV
description:
Compare current valuation with
movement-based cost
MVRV divides market capitalization by realized capitalization using compatible series. It
summarizes valuation relative to an on-chain cost-basis proxy without supplying a universal
market-top threshold.
method:
MVRV = CapMrktCurUSD / CapRealUSD.
Coin Metrics matched market/realized-cap convention selected for reproducibility. Glassnode offers related variants that must
not be silently mixed.
interpretation:
BTC sits above its aggregate movement-based cost proxy. Cross-asset ratios require compatible
methods and cannot be treated like directly comparable earnings multiples.

name: MVRV Z Score
description:
Standardize the valuation gap with an
explicit history
MVRV Z-score divides the market-minus-realized-cap gap by historical market-cap dispersion.
It is not the ordinary z-score of the MVRV ratio itself.
method:
MVRV_Z = (MarketCap_t - RealizedCap_t) / SD(MarketCap_start,...,MarketCap_t).
Glassnode published expanding-history metric is the replication target. A house reconstruction uses population SD (n
denominator) and stores the first available date; it is labeled separately.
interpretation:
The valuation gap is large relative to a particular historical scale. Starting the history at a
different date changes that scale and the resulting score.

name: SOPR
description:
Read spent-coin profitability without
assuming every spend is a sale
SOPR compares USD value at spending with USD value at creation for the same spent outputs.
The ratio-of-sums convention weights by economic size rather than treating all outputs
equally.
method:
SOPR = sum RealizedValueUSD(spent outputs) / sum CreationValueUSD(those spent
outputs).
Glassnode spent-output profit ratio aggregation.
interpretation:
The spent set carries gains under the movement-based accounting model. Custody reshuffles
can realize the metric without a market sale.

name: NUPL
description:
Estimate aggregate unrealized gains
under the chosen cost proxy
NUPL scales the market-minus-realized-cap gap by market capitalization. It summarizes the
fraction of current value above or below the on-chain cost proxy.
method:
NUPL = (MarketCap - RealizedCap) / MarketCap.
Glassnode net-unrealized-profit/loss identity.
interpretation:
The network's accounting proxy indicates net unrealized gains. Cohort, age and ownership
distribution are needed to investigate supply behavior.

name: NVT
description:
Compare network valuation with
economic transfer activity
NVT divides market value by adjusted on-chain transfer value for a declared interval. It relates
valuation to settlement activity, not to protocol profit or exchange trading volume.
method:
NVT_daily = CapMrktCurUSD / TxTfrValAdjUSD_daily.
House daily ratio using matched Coin Metrics series. This selects an adjusted-transfer convention; alternative NVT smoothers
and entity filters are distinct.
interpretation:
High NVT can mean high valuation, low settlement activity or a different usage mix. Daily
transfer spikes can temporarily compress it.

name: Adjusted Transfer Value
description:
Remove accounting churn before
interpreting transfer value
Adjusted transfer value attempts to isolate economically meaningful movement from raw
ledger transfers. This book selects Coin Metrics' published adjusted series rather than claiming
to reproduce opaque entity heuristics.
method:
Production method: read Coin Metrics TxTfrValAdjUSD at asset/date/frequency/version.
Conceptually: sum of transfers retained by the asset-specific CM adjustment method,
valued in USD.
The exact operational method is the named provider series. The worked filter is illustrative, not a claim to reproduce CM's
chain-specific heuristics.
interpretation:
A busy chain may contain operational recycling. Adjustments improve interpretation but
remain methodology-dependent and can be revised.

name: Active Addresses or Active Entities
description:
Count active addresses without counting
them as people
Active-address counts deduplicate addresses participating under a provider's eligibility rules.
Entity counts add a clustering model; neither measure directly identifies unique human users.
method:
Active addresses = cardinality(union of eligible senders and receivers in T).
Active entities = cardinality(provider clusters represented in that set).
Coin Metrics AdrActCnt is the selected address series; entity counts are explicitly separate, provider-defined estimates. Asset
inclusion rules are retained.
interpretation:
Activity shows use of addresses. Bots, contracts and one actor using several wallets can
produce apparent adoption.

name: Transaction Count
description:
Separate transaction throughput from
economic adoption
Transaction count measures confirmed ledger transactions under declared inclusion rules. It
counts ledger objects, not users, token transfers or economically independent decisions.
method:
TransactionCount_T = number of eligible confirmed ledger transactions in T.
Coin Metrics TxCnt selected with asset-specific inclusion rules. The simplified calculation demonstrates filtering only, not a
universal exclusion list.
interpretation:
More transactions can indicate economic demand, automated farming, batching changes or
protocol mechanics. Fees and user persistence help distinguish them.

name: Velocity
description:
Express how rapidly network value
circulates
Velocity is adjusted transfer value divided by market value over a stated interval. It is the
reciprocal of NVT only when the exact same inputs and horizon are used.
method:
Velocity = AdjustedTransferValueUSD / MarketCap = 1/NVT under matching
numerator/denominator convention.
Glassnode identity when NVT uses the same adjusted transfer value.
interpretation:
Higher movement relative to value may mean productive settlement or rapid recycling. It is not
automatically stronger investment demand.

name: Whale Transfer Share
description:
Locate concentration in large transfers
Whale transfer share measures the fraction of eligible transfer value above a declared size
cutoff. It classifies transaction size, not the identity, skill or intent of the actor.
interpretation:
Activity is concentrated in large transfers. Operational contracts and custodians can dominate
this measure without a directional view.

name: Holder Concentration
description:
Measure ownership concentration while
respecting custody
Holder HHI sums squared balance shares over a declared holder universe. Excluding
exchanges or contracts changes the economic question and requires renormalizing the
remaining balances.
method:
HolderHHI = sum_i s_i^2, s_i=balance_i/sum_j balance_j after an explicitly documented
exclusion universe.
HHI concentration on labeled non-contract/non-exchange holders when exclusions are enabled; raw- holder version also
stored.
interpretation:
Large addresses do not map cleanly to beneficial owners. Custodians aggregate many people;
one actor may split holdings across wallets.

name: Token Unlock Pressure
description:
Measure scheduled supply without
assuming immediate selling
Unlock pressure compares scheduled newly transferable token value with current circulating
capitalization. It measures potential supply availability over a fixed horizon, not guaranteed
market sales.
method:
UnlockPressure_H = ScheduledUnlockUSD_(t,t+H] / CirculatingMarketCapUSD_t.
DefiLlama-style scheduled unlock data; H=30 calendar days in the standard report and is metadata, not a buy/sell threshold.
interpretation:
An unlock can expand transferable supply. Recipients may hold, hedge, stake or transfer, so
selling pressure remains conditional.

name: Fee and Revenue Trend
description:
Separate user payments from value
retained by the protocol
Fee and revenue trends compare like-for-like periods and accounting scopes. Under the
selected DefiLlama definition, revenue excludes supply-side payouts; protocol and
token-holder allocations require separate attention.
method:
Revenue = Fees - SupplySideRevenue.
Growth_30d = sum(last 30 complete days) / sum(previous 30 complete days) - 1.
DefiLlama selected accounting convention; revenue excludes suppliers. Track protocol retention and token-holder allocations
separately; zero/negative prior revenue requires a non-ratio report.
interpretation:
Activity may be improving while token-holder value capture remains unchanged. Fees,
revenue, earnings and distributions answer different questions.

name: TVL and TVL Change
description:
Separate deposited capital from the price
of collateral
TVL values the assets included by a protocol's accounting methodology. Changes combine
token-balance movements and prices, so TVL growth is not the same as net deposits.
method:
TVL_t = sum_(eligible assets j) q_(j,t) P_(j,t).
TVL growth = TVL_t/TVL_(t-k)-1.
DefiLlama inclusion and double-counting policy selected. Store token quantities, prices and category toggles; TVL growth is not
net capital inflow.
interpretation:
The protocol looks larger in dollars, yet no additional assets were deposited. Token-balance
and price contributions must be disentangled.

name: Stablecoin Liquidity Context
description:
Track stablecoin supply without
assuming deployable demand
Stablecoin liquidity context measures changes in a declared supply universe. Supply growth is
potential liquidity, not a direct observation that capital will buy BTC or an altcoin.
method:
StablecoinLiquidityGrowth = StablecoinSupplyUSD_t / StablecoinSupplyUSD_(t-k) - 1 for
the declared chain/universe.
DefiLlama stablecoin circulating-supply context; chain attribution and bridged assets follow provider definitions.
interpretation:
More settlement liquidity can support activity, but balances may remain idle, fund collateral or
move through arbitrage.

name: BTC Dominance
description:
Read BTC dominance as a ratio with a
moving denominator
BTC dominance is Bitcoin circulating capitalization divided by total eligible crypto
capitalization. It reflects relative valuation and universe construction, not a direct
measurement of capital flows.
method:
BTCDominance = BTC_CirculatingMarketCap / TotalCryptoCirculatingMarketCap * 100.
Consistent market-cap provider and universe; stablecoins/wrapped duplicates inclusion policy stored.
interpretation:
Alts grew faster in aggregate. The ratio cannot distinguish new issuance, price repricing and
actual portfolio rotation.

name: Advance Decline Breadth
description:
Check whether the rally reaches most
assets
Advance-decline breadth compares the number of rising and falling assets. Equal-count
breadth counterbalances a capitalization-weighted headline dominated by a few large tokens.
method:
AD_Breadth = (N_advance - N_decline)/(N_advance+N_decline); unchanged assets excluded
from denominator.
Equal-count breadth on a survivorship-controlled universe.
interpretation:
Positive breadth supports wider participation. It is stronger evidence when the rising assets are
liquid and the universe was fixed beforehand.

name: Percent Above Moving Average
description:
Measure how widely the trend is
established
Percent above a moving average counts assets above a declared trailing price baseline. It
measures breadth of trend state, not the probability that the trend will continue.
method:
PctAboveMA = 100 * count_i(P_i > MA_i) / N_valid.
Equal-count breadth; moving-average horizon is a parameter stored in metadata.
interpretation:
Many valid assets show an established upward state. Missingness can still bias the apparent
strength.

name: Cross Sectional Dispersion
description:
Measure how unevenly the market is
moving
Cross-sectional dispersion is the standard deviation of same-period returns across assets. It
describes differences within the market and is distinct from volatility through time.
method:
CrossSectionalDispersion_t = sqrt[sum_i (R_i,t - R_bar_t)^2/(N-1)].
Equal-weight sample SD of same-horizon asset returns.
interpretation:
A green market headline does not imply a uniform opportunity set. High dispersion makes
asset selection and residual explanations more important.

name: Sector Relative Strength
description:
Compare a sector with BTC on a relative
wealth basis
Sector relative strength here is log sector return minus log BTC return. It measures relative
performance without dividing by a return that may be zero or negative.
method:
SectorRelativeReturn = ln(1+R_sector) - ln(1+R_BTC).
Log relative performance avoids ratio pathologies when returns are negative.
interpretation:
The sector gained relative wealth against BTC. Exposure, composition changes and genuine
sector news can all contribute.

name: Cross Sectional Momentum Rank
description:
Rank momentum while retaining the
absolute return
Momentum percentile places an asset's trailing total return within a declared universe. A high
rank is relative strength; it can coexist with a negative absolute return.
method:
Momentum_i = product_(s=t-W+1..t)(1+R_(i,s))-1.
Percentile_i = 100 x (ascending average rank_i - 1)/(N-1).
House equal-count percentile; average ranks for ties, predeclared lookback and point-in-time eligible universe. N<2 yields
unavailable.
interpretation:
Relative leadership does not prove buying pressure sufficient to overcome the market. The BTC
regime remains relevant to the absolute outcome.

name: Market Concentration HHI
description:
Measure how much the market depends
on a few names
Market HHI sums squared capitalization shares and scales the result to 0-10,000. It describes
concentration of valuation, not directly correlation or concentration of beneficial ownership.
method:
HHI = 10,000 * sum_i s_i^2, s_i=market_cap_i/sum_j market_cap_j.
DOJ-style 0-10,000 scaling applied to crypto market-cap shares.
interpretation:
Many listed tokens do not guarantee a balanced capitalization index. A few names can
determine most of its behavior.

name: Correlation Dispersion
description:
Find whether BTC relationships are
uniformly tight or uneven
Correlation dispersion is the sample standard deviation of asset-to-BTC correlations across a
fixed universe. It reveals heterogeneity in relationships, not the level of diversification by itself.
method:
CorrDispersion = SD({ρ_i,BTC}) across assets i in the universe, using the same
rolling window.
House sample-SD convention for benchmark correlations; also publish median/IQR.
interpretation:
The market's relationships are uneven. Low dispersion could mean everything is tightly
coupled or everything is weakly coupled, so median correlation is essential context.
